strengths: The paper targets an important problem in crystal property prediction and makes a plausible high-level case that reciprocal-space information can complement local graph encoders for long-range periodic structure modeling.

The proposed architecture is clearly motivated as a fusion of graph embeddings with learned diffraction-like features, and the manuscript includes ablations over the diffraction module, attention heads, residual connections, edge features, pseudo-particle versus tabulated X-ray factors, and number of Miller indices.
The empirical scope is broad, covering Materials Project, JARVIS-DFT, and several Matbench tasks, with comparisons to many standard crystal GNN/Transformer baselines.
The reported results, if validated, would be practically meaningful: PRDNet improves several energy, band gap, elastic-property, and classification metrics across datasets.
weaknesses: Several central theoretical claims are overstated or technically questionable. Diffraction is claimed to be a unique, non-lossy representation, but finite sampled structure factors, learned form factors, and diffraction phase/ambiguity issues do not justify this. The paper does not rigorously prove uniqueness for the actual representation used by PRDNet.

The invariance argument appears flawed. The action on Miller indices is not carefully defined, the proof mixes translations into reciprocal-index transformations, and flattening ordered real/imaginary structure factors over H is not automatically invariant to rotations/reflections unless the representation is canonically ordered or symmetrically aggregated. This undermines a core claimed property of the method.

The evaluation protocol lacks key details needed for a top-tier empirical claim: train/validation/test splits, Matbench cross-validation compliance, hyperparameter tuning policy for PRDNet, random seeds, variance/error bars, and whether results are averaged over folds or runs.

A directly relevant baseline, ReGNet, is discussed and criticized but not included in the experimental tables. This is a major omission because the claimed contribution is specifically reciprocal-space modeling for crystals.

The comparison may be unfair or hard to interpret because baseline implementations are described as using original/default settings rather than consistently tuned settings under the same splits and budget. Some baseline numbers also look unexpectedly weak for modern models on certain tasks, requiring stronger validation.

Reproducibility is limited: the code is only promised after acceptance, implementation details for the proposed model are incomplete, and computational cost/memory/runtime analyses are absent despite potentially expensive Miller-index structure-factor computation.

The ablation results show very large drops from removing individual components, but there is no statistical analysis, no uncertainty estimates, and no discussion of whether the graph-only variant is capacity-matched to the full model.

The method section contains notation and formulation issues, such as repeated query concatenation in the attention equation, unclear dimensionalities, inconsistent use of fractional versus Cartesian coordinates, and learned form factors that depend on graph embeddings while being presented as physically constrained diffraction quantities.

The writing sometimes overclaims physical grounding: the pseudo-particle is learned for prediction performance, but the manuscript frames it as more sensitive than any physical particle without a clear physical or mathematical basis beyond supervised accuracy.

Ethical and practical considerations are minimal; while risks are limited for materials prediction, the paper should discuss limitations around dataset bias, DFT label noise, failed generalization to out-of-distribution chemistries, and possible misuse of predictive confidence in materials screening.

strengths: The paper targets an important problem in crystal property prediction and identifies a real limitation of finite-cutoff real-space GNNs for long-range periodic interactions.
The high-level idea of augmenting graph representations with reciprocal-space/structure-factor features is plausible and relevant to materials ML.

The manuscript evaluates on several commonly used materials benchmarks and includes ablations for the diffraction module, attention heads, residual connections, edge features, and learned versus tabulated form factors.
weaknesses: The central theoretical claim that the proposed diffraction representation is physically guaranteed to be unique is not justified. The model uses a finite set of Miller indices and learned form factors derived from a local GNN, which does not provide an injective representation of crystal structures.

The invariance argument appears technically flawed. Flattening real and imaginary components over an ordered Miller-index set is generally equivariant to index permutations, not invariant, unless the architecture explicitly pools or canonicalizes over symmetry orbits. The proof also treats translation phases and crystallographic operations too simplistically, especially for fractional translations, screw axes, and glide planes.

The method description has several mathematical inconsistencies or ambiguities, including vector-valued attention scores without a clear normalization/softmax, repeated query concatenation, unclear dimensionalities, and unclear handling of complex phases and index ordering.

The learned pseudo-particle is presented as physically motivated, but it is essentially a learned feature transform. The paper overstates physical fidelity and sensitivity relative to real probes without adequate theoretical or experimental support.

The empirical evaluation is not sufficiently reproducible: code is withheld until acceptance, data splits are not clearly specified, seed variance and statistical significance are missing, and many implementation details needed to reproduce the exact benchmark setup are absent.

Baseline comparisons are questionable. The paper uses different losses, schedules, epochs, and hyperparameters across models, says baselines use original settings without tuning, and does not convincingly establish fair model selection. Direct comparison to the closely related ReGNet is discussed conceptually but not included experimentally.

The Matbench evaluation appears incomplete or nonstandard: the paper reports single numbers rather than the standard cross-validation protocol and does not clearly state folds, splits, or leaderboard-compatible evaluation procedures.

Several reported gains are suspiciously large in ablations, especially the dramatic degradation from replacing learned form factors with X-ray factors or removing diffraction, without enough diagnostics to rule out confounding from capacity, optimization, or leakage-like split artifacts.

The paper’s positioning is overstated. Prior reciprocal-space and long-range periodic models are not adequately compared, and claims of state-of-the-art performance and physical uniqueness exceed the evidence provided.

Presentation quality is weak for a top-tier submission, with typos, formatting issues, inconsistent naming, unclear equations, and imprecise physical language that make it hard to assess the contribution reliably.

strengths: The paper proposes a clear and interesting idea: augmenting crystal graph representations with learned reciprocal-space diffraction features, using pseudo-particle form factors to capture environment-dependent scattering beyond tabulated X-ray factors.
weaknesses: The strongest theoretical claims are overstated. The asserted uniqueness of the diffraction representation is not rigorously established for finite sampled Miller indices, learned form factors, and the usual phase ambiguities of diffraction-like representations. The invariance proof is also not fully convincing: flattening real and imaginary structure factors over a symmetry-closed index set yields at best a permutation/equivariance issue unless the downstream processing is permutation invariant or canonicalized, which is not shown. Translation invariance is especially questionable because real/imaginary structure factors generally acquire phase shifts under origin changes.

strengths: The paper targets an important problem in crystal property prediction and proposes an intuitively appealing combination of real-space graph features with reciprocal-space diffraction features.
The experimental section is broad, covering Materials Project, JARVIS-DFT, MatBench, and an additional JARVIS-DFT-3D-2021 setting, with comparisons to many relevant crystal GNN/transformer baselines.

The ablations are useful in spirit: they evaluate removal of the diffraction module, attention heads, residual connections, edge features, number of Miller indices, and learned pseudo-particle versus tabulated X-ray form factors.
The reported empirical results are often strong, especially on MP and several JARVIS/MatBench targets, suggesting that the added diffraction-style features may be practically useful.
weaknesses: Several central theoretical claims are overstated or technically incorrect. The paper claims physically guaranteed uniqueness/completeness of the diffraction representation, but finite reciprocal samples and diffraction-style representations do not generally guarantee uniqueness; phase ambiguity and homometric structures are not addressed.

The invariance argument is not convincing. Flattening real and imaginary structure factors over a Miller-index set that is merely closed under symmetry yields permutations and phase changes, not an invariant representation unless an invariant aggregation or canonical ordering is proved. The treatment of translations and crystallographic operations in Eq. 18-19 is also mathematically confused.

The proposed pseudo-particle form factor is described as depending on |Q|, local environment, and species, but the implementation equation maps node embeddings directly to per-index outputs and does not clearly encode the reciprocal-lattice metric or true scattering-vector magnitude. This weakens the claimed physical interpretation.

The method section has ambiguities and possible errors, e.g. repeated query concatenation in Eq. 9, no clear softmax normalization for attention, undefined beta/gating details, and unclear handling of variable numbers/orderings of Miller indices and crystal cells.

The empirical comparison is difficult to fully trust. PRDNet has 20.9M parameters, substantially larger than most baselines, and the paper does not adequately disentangle gains from capacity, training budget, or tuning. Some baselines are reimplemented by the authors, trained on different GPUs, and may not be equally optimized.

Reproducibility is incomplete despite the statement: the abstract says code is available but the URL is missing, dataset split details are not consistently specified for all benchmarks, and there are no uncertainty estimates or repeated-run statistics.

The paper’s positioning against prior reciprocal-space methods is too dismissive and partly relies on unproven physical assertions. The relationship to Crystalformer/reciprocal attention, EwaldMP, PotNet, and ReGNet needs a more careful technical comparison.
Writing and presentation contain many clarity issues and typos, and some claims are much stronger than the evidence supports, especially around uniqueness, physical validity, and invariance.

strengths: The paper targets an important problem in crystal property prediction: representing long-range periodic interactions beyond local graph neighborhoods.
The idea of combining real-space graph embeddings with reciprocal-space or diffraction-inspired features is relevant and could be useful if formulated and evaluated carefully.
The empirical section covers many standard materials datasets and compares against a broad set of graph, transformer, and reciprocal-space baselines.
The ablations attempt to isolate the diffraction module, attention heads, residual connections, and edge features, and the reported numbers suggest the proposed components may help.
weaknesses: The central theoretical claims are substantially overstated. The paper repeatedly claims a lossless, unique, physically guaranteed diffraction representation, but the implemented representation uses a finite selected set of Miller indices and learned form factors derived from graph embeddings, so it is not generally injective or physically guaranteed.

The invariance argument appears flawed. A crystallographic operation generally permutes Miller indices, but the paper flattens real and imaginary components into an ordered vector and feeds them to an MLP; without permutation-invariant aggregation over the index orbit, the representation is not invariant. The claim of full E(3) invariance is also not justified by equations written in fractional coordinates tied to the lattice basis.

The proof around translation phases is questionable: the paper asserts the phase is always integer, but fractional translations from screw/glide operations and origin shifts can induce nontrivial phases. Moreover, using real and imaginary structure factors rather than intensities makes phase conventions important.

The method is positioned as physically grounded diffraction, but the learned pseudo-particle form factor is essentially an MLP output indexed by Miller reflections. This weakens the physical interpretation and makes the distinction from generic Fourier/reciprocal features unclear.

The empirical evaluation is not fully convincing. PRDNet has far more parameters than many baselines, and improvements may partly reflect capacity or tuning rather than the proposed diffraction mechanism. There is no careful parameter-matched or compute-matched comparison.

Several baseline results appear weaker than commonly reported numbers or are reproduced by the authors under unclear settings. For ReGNet/ReciNet, the code is said to be unavailable and the authors use their own implementation, which makes the comparison less reliable.
The Matbench evaluation does not clearly follow the official Matbench cross-validation protocol and leaderboard reporting; random or nonstandard splits would make the results difficult to compare.
No uncertainty estimates, multiple seeds, or statistical significance analyses are reported, despite small margins on several tasks.

The ablations are too coarse. Removing the diffraction branch also changes parameterization and information flow, and there is no comparison to simpler Fourier features, fixed XRD-like form factors, randomized reciprocal features, or structure-factor magnitudes/intensities.

Reproducibility is weak: the abstract and dataset descriptions contain missing links, implementation details are incomplete, and the claimed open code is not actually specified in the manuscript text provided.

Presentation quality is poor in places, with formatting problems, typos, inconsistent naming such as Crystalframer/Crystalfarmer and ReGNet/ReciNet, awkward grammar, and equations with unclear or inconsistent notation.

The paper makes broad claims about existing methods mapping distinct crystals to identical representations, but the examples and discussion are not rigorous enough to establish this as a decisive limitation of current state-of-the-art models.

strengths: Addresses an important problem in crystal property prediction: augmenting local graph encoders with reciprocal-space information to capture longer-range periodic structure.
The pseudo-particle diffraction idea is creative and physically motivated, and the paper makes a plausible case that learned form factors can be more task-relevant than fixed X-ray form factors.

Empirical evaluation is broad, covering Materials Project, JARVIS-DFT, JARVIS-DFT-3D-2021, and several MatBench tasks, with generally strong results across energy, band gap, mechanical, optical, and classification targets.
Ablations are useful and consistently support the contribution of the diffraction module, multi-head attention, residual updates, and edge features.

The paper includes implementation details, hyperparameter descriptions, and additional baseline-plus-diffraction experiments, which improve reproducibility and help isolate the value of the proposed module.
weaknesses: Some theoretical claims are overstated. The assertion that diffraction gives a unique or lossless crystal representation is too strong without carefully addressing phase ambiguity, finite Miller-index truncation, origin choice, and non-isomorphic structures with similar or identical diffraction signatures.

The invariance argument appears incomplete or possibly flawed. A general translation induces a phase shift in complex structure factors, so using real and imaginary components directly is not obviously translation invariant; the claim that the phase is always an integer only holds under restrictive crystallographic operations, not arbitrary coordinate-origin shifts.

The Miller-index closure construction using signs and permutations does not convincingly cover all relevant lattice symmetries for arbitrary crystals, and the mapping between real-space rotations/reflections and reciprocal-space index permutations is underdeveloped.

Comparisons are strong but not fully controlled: PRDNet has substantially more parameters than most baselines, some baselines are reimplemented or not equally tuned, GPU settings vary in supplemental experiments, and ReGNet results rely partly on the authors’ own implementation.
The MatBench evaluation does not clearly state whether official cross-validation protocols and test-server procedures are followed, which matters for comparability.

Several reported gains may partly come from added capacity and fusion architecture rather than the claimed physically unique reciprocal representation; stronger capacity-matched ablations and runtime/memory analysis would make the case more convincing.

Writing and notation contain inconsistencies and minor errors, including ambiguous equations in the attention block, occasional typos, and some missing or unclear repository/dataset links in the extracted manuscript.
